speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We continually look for opportunities to drive work to Singapore and Singaporeans, keep abreast of developments in other jurisdictions and also update our regime so that we can continue to remain an attractive place for businesses to want to be at and to deal with and address their legal needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Singapore is recognised as a premier legal services hub, in Asia and also the rest of the world.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In 2021, Singapore was, for the first time, selected as the most preferred seat of arbitration in the world, alongside London, in the Queen Mary University of London and White and Case International Arbitration Survey.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is a fine achievement, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic, which has itself presented new challenges.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Even so, Sir, we cannot afford to rest on our laurels.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is imperative for us to continually review, strengthen and update our framework, in order to stay competitive and meet the needs of businesses and users alike.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Bill also makes a miscellaneous amendment to clarify the date certain provisions relating to the regulation of foreign lawyers and foreign law practice entities were operationalised following the transfer of relevant regulatory functions from the Attorney-General to the Director of Legal Services on 18 November 2015.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The introduction of a CFA framework builds on our reforms in the litigation funding space, to enhance our offerings as a dispute resolution hub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To set the context, I will provide some background on litigation funding in Singapore, before going into the proposed legislative framework for CFAs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Broadly, litigation funding refers to methods of funding legal proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In Singapore, lawyers’ costs are typically paid by the client, as we have, historically, been more conservative about litigation funding.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is due to traditional prohibitions against maintenance and champerty, concepts which we have ourselves inherited from the English common law system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These rules were originally developed to guard against officious intermeddling in litigation and potential conflicts of interest, which lawyers providing financial assistance may face vis-à-vis their duty to their own clients, who may be vulnerable litigants, and also to the Court.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, we have been taking incremental steps and looking at the landscape holistically.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As legal costs can be substantial, we have observed a growing trend of alternative funding methods internationally.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have, therefore, been studying how to better meet the needs of businesses and individuals and also enhance access to justice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have taken into account what has been done elsewhere in other jurisdictions – the safeguards that have been implemented, some of the learned experiences that they have since implementing and working out how we can better contextualise them for use in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: One area of reform we have introduced is in third-party funding (TPF), where a party unconnected to the dispute funds the claim, usually in exchange for a share of the damages awarded if the claim succeeds.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Since then, funders have reported an upturn in requests for funding in Singapore, with funding provided in some cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The legal and funding communities also shared that the reforms have been useful and beneficial.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have, therefore, extended the framework in June 2021 to domestic arbitration, certain proceedings in the SICC and also related Court and mediation proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Apart from the above, we also observed interest and needs for TPF in certain insolvency-related matters before the Courts and various reforms were worked into our insolvency legislation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Given the positive feedback received from the TPF reforms, with few risks and downsides observed, we have continued to study other potential reforms in the litigation funding space.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This includes CFAs, which are the focus of this Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: CFAs are arrangements where a lawyer receives payment of a part, or all, of his or her legal fees only in specified agreed circumstances, such as when the client’s claim is successful.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: CFAs may take the form of a “no win, no fee”, or “no win, less fee” agreement, depending on how the fees are to be paid to the lawyer if the claim is unsuccessful.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: CFAs and contingency fees are, currently, prohibited and unenforceable in Singapore, under the rules against maintenance and champerty, which I referred to earlier.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, it updates our litigation funding framework and aligns it with developments and practices on the international front.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This helps to enhance the competitiveness and vibrancy of our legal industry and landscape.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: While Singapore lawyers are currently not allowed to offer CFAs, other common law jurisdictions have already moved away from these traditional prohibitions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For instance, England and Wales abolished the prohibitions in the 1990s and, together with the United States, Australia and Canada, allow CFAs in various forms today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Oftentimes, our lawyers compete on an international front internationally with foreign lawyers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In other jurisdictions, they can offer CFAs whilst our lawyers are not able to offer CFAs as part of their engagement with their clients.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, allowing CFAs can also enhance access to justice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is particularly pertinent with current business interruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Businesses with legitimate claims, but themselves facing cash flow problems, may not be able to put out full legal fees at the outset.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: CFAs will help provide such claimants with an alternative method of funding meritorious claims, which they may otherwise not be able to pursue.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In jurisdictions that allow CFAs, other advantages have also been observed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As lawyers are typically better placed to evaluate the legal risks of a claim, compared to clients, sharing of financial risks of litigation between client and lawyer can also be beneficial.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Just as CFAs can enable pursuit of meritorious cases, they can also discourage the pursuit of weak cases and frivolous claims, as lawyers’ fees are contingent on the outcome of the claim Sir, we studied the approaches taken in other jurisdictions and sought feedback from stakeholders via a public and closed consultations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Having carefully reviewed all the feedback received and looked at the landscape and studied the outcomes in various other jurisdictions, we have designed a framework for CFAs in Singapore as set out in this Bill which, we believe, best allows us to make an initial move on CFAs whilst, at the same time, studying the impact it may have on a broader litigation funding landscape.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clauses 3 to 6 of the Bill set out the overarching framework for CFAs, while further details and safeguards will be prescribed in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Broadly, Sir, clause 3 states that lawyers will not be prevented from entering into a CFA that complies with the new Part 8A in the Legal Profession Act (LPA), where the CFA framework will be housed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 4 amends existing section 111 in Part 8 of the LPA, to clarify that Part 8 of the LPA does not apply to an agreement which is a CFA that complies with the new Part 8A.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 6 sets out the proposed Part 8A of the LPA, which will provide the main framework for CFAs in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The proposed Part 8A will have six new sections, sections 115A to 115F.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Section 115A defines key terms in the CFA framework and sets out the scope of Part 8A.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In that regard, similar to Part 8 of the LPA, Part 8A will apply to Singapore law practices and certain registered foreign lawyers and foreign law practices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Section 115B creates a statutory exception for CFAs that comply with prescribed requirements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To be clear, Sir, the statutory framework for CFAs is not intended to override existing common law principles on CFAs relating to impecunious clients, which can continue to provide access to justice for such litigants.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: CFAs will be enforceable only in prescribed proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As a start, we intend to prescribe the following proceedings by way of subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These will be, as Members may recall, the same categories as the extended TPF framework that we have put in place.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are concurrently studying the feasibility of allowing CFAs in other categories of proceedings, such as domestic proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The rationale for an extension of the framework would be aimed at uplifting the legal profession to further enhance and pursue access to justice for more litigants, who may otherwise not have such access.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But as these proceedings may involve more vulnerable litigants, we will study it more carefully.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We intend to closely consult all relevant stakeholders in the legal industry and other interested parties before making a move on this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Section 115B(6) provides that the range of work that can be covered by a CFA include (a) work done for the purposes of, and before, contemplated proceedings, such as preliminary advice, negotiations or the settlement of disputes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Oftentimes, these are matters which are a precursor to the substantive work, and the framework provides that the CFA can cover this kind of work as well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is even if those proceedings are not eventually commenced, or if the claim or dispute in those proceedings is settled.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But, obviously, in those cases, the terms of the CFA must appropriately reflect the specific conditions on which the uplift or the additional fee structure can then be triggered.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Another key feature of the CFA framework is that “uplift fees” may be provided.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Section 115A(1) provides for a definition for this “uplift fee”, which are the fees payable to the lawyer in specified circumstances, that are higher than what would have otherwise been payable if there were no CFA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The lawyer and client may and should agree on the specific circumstances under which the uplift fee should be paid.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These circumstances can be amended as the case progresses, if agreed, because basically, the CFA is an agreement between the parties – the lawyer and his client – and these agreements can be varied or altered from time to time, subject to there being consensus by the parties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As I have said, because the CFA is, in essence, a contract between a lawyer and his client, parties would be free to determine a mutually agreeable arrangement for the payment of fees, subject to the prescribed requirements in our framework.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As in any contract, the parties should ensure that the terms are sufficiently clear, which may include scenarios for when such a contract might be terminated.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I also wish to make clear that the CFAs are not intended to replace traditional fee structures but, instead, provide an additional funding option between a lawyer and his client.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Lawyers and clients can agree on a traditional fee structure in one area of work, and a CFA in another.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, it can be a combination of both free structures, or it might also seek to convert one to the other – either way, depending on the circumstances.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There is no impediment to usual payment practices, such as collecting deposits for fees, except that no deposit should be collected for the uplifted portion, which depends on the triggering of a condition which will take place on a subsequent occasion.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Parties may agree to include or exclude the payment of disbursements from the CFA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, that is entirely up to the parties' choice and the terms they seek to write into the CFA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Lawyers and clients should also discuss and provide for how and when a CFA may be terminated and the fees to be paid should the CFA be terminated prematurely.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is for obvious reasons so that you have clarity upfront because, sometimes, the client may decide to choose a different lawyer halfway through the proceedings and you do not want the fact that there is a CFA cloud the question as to what the appropriate amount of fees is to be paid at that juncture.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Bill and subsidiary legislation will introduce safeguards to mitigate the risk of any potential abuse of the CFAs by lawyers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, under section 115B, a CFA must meet certain requirements for it to be valid.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It should not provide for remuneration and costs to be a proportion of the amount recovered by the client in the litigation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, for example, it cannot be a proportion of the damages that a client might recover.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Such arrangements, which are often known as contingency fee agreements, will continue to be prohibited in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The reason for this is because the payment received by lawyers in such agreements has no direct correlation with the work done.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The amount of damages that the client may recover is dependent on the client's particular circumstances and the damage and injuries that may be suffered.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If you allow such proportions to be part of the CFA, this may give rise to added risks of conflicts of interests for the lawyer.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will continue to study developments in this area.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Third, the CFA must comply with the regulations that will be made under section 115B(7).

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These include: (a) information that the lawyer must provide to the client, for instance, how the CFA operates and how uplift fees are calculated in a particular case; (b) terms and conditions that must be included in the CFA, such as a “cooling-off” period after the CFA is entered into, during which the client or lawyer may terminate the CFA by giving written notice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Lawyers will continue to be subject to the Legal Profession (Professional Conduct) Rules (PCR), including obligations to: (a) act in the best interests of their clients; (b) evaluate whether any consequence of a matter involving the client justifies the expense or the risk of pursuing the matter; (c) withdraw from representing a client in certain circumstances due to, say, ethical reasons – these are obligations and responsibilities which a lawyer will be very familiar with; and, finally, of course, (d) an obligation not to overcharge.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will be clarified in amendments to the PCR.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MinLaw will also be working with the Law Society to develop a Guidance Note on CFAs, with the aim of guiding the profession through these new developments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MinLaw will also continue to review the landscape and the use of CFAs in practice and may also develop additional and different safeguards for different categories of proceedings as may be appropriate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They are adapted from the current Part 8 of the LPA but with modifications, and cover matters, such as: (a) the effect of the CFA on legal costs, (b) how the validity or effect of a CFA is to be assessed, and (c) the consequences of a change in, the death, incapacity or winding up of, a solicitor or law practice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This seeks to avoid the issues of satellite litigation faced by other jurisdictions, where it has been noted that CFAs were challenged by the unsuccessful party, to avoid paying uplift fees to a successful party as part of legal costs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, in other jurisdictions, if the uplifted fees are payable as part of party-and-party costs, it provides an opportunity for there to be additional litigation for the losing party to challenge the validity and application of the CFA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, section 115D concerns questions on the validity and enforceability of a CFA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In determining such questions, the Court will examine whether the requirements of a CFA as set out in section 115B have been met, and whether the CFA is void or voidable based on usual contractual principles, such as incapacity, mistake, misrepresentation and so on.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Court will also have regard to the circumstances in which the agreement was made and the interests of all parties to the agreement, that is, the client and the lawyer, taken as a whole.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Court should also consider the purpose and context of a CFA when determining its enforceability.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As an example, the mere fact of an uplift should not call the CFA into question, although the amount of uplift should be commensurate with the risk undertaken by the lawyer.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As the CFA is a contract between the client and the lawyer, such an approach is based on well-established contractual principles and provides certainty to parties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 2 seeks to refine the scope of representation of a foreign lawyer in certain proceedings in the SICC, particularly international corporate debt restructuring and insolvency cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In the last five years, we have made tremendous progress to our corporate debt restructuring and insolvency regime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our laws have remained progressive, open and modern, whilst balancing the interests of creditors, debtors and other stakeholders, all of whom have an interest in particularly large, cross-border, complex insolvencies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The proposed amendment seeks to build on this momentum and enhance Singapore as a premier centre for debt restructuring and insolvency matters both regionally, as well as globally, internationally.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Such matters typically involve a multi-jurisdiction dimension and significant foreign elements, including proceedings in foreign courts, which may otherwise not be heard in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The SICC was identified by the Committee to Strengthen Singapore as an International Centre for Debt Restructuring in 2016, as a conducive forum to hear insolvency matters with international elements and multi-jurisdictional issues.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The SICC was established in 2015 to hear transnational and commercial disputes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It broadens and complements existing dispute resolution options.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The proposed refinements leverage on SICC's strengths and attractive infrastructure and seeks to facilitate the efficient and effective presentation of arguments and resolution of debt restructuring and insolvency proceedings in the SICC.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, the SICC's jurisdiction over international restructuring and insolvency cases was clarified by the Courts (Civil and Criminal Justice) Reform Act 2021.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And in connection with that, clause 2 of this Bill proposes to refine the scope of a foreign lawyer's representation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Corporate debt restructuring and insolvency work can be complex, and proceedings will often involve transnational and interconnected issues, with mixed issues of foreign and local law, along with mixed issues of law and fact.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The proposed refinements here seek to facilitate collaboration between local and foreign lawyers for the efficient and fair resolution of such cases before the SICC.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In turn, it will benefit litigants and other stakeholders and support the growth of international cases being heard in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, subsidiary legislation may provide for the various categories of specified proceedings that these refinements will apply to; factors that the Court may consider in deciding whether to grant permission to the foreign lawyer; and exceptions to any of these restrictions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, these are the points that will be dealt with in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will align this Bill with the Courts (Civil and Criminal Justice) Reform Act 2021 that I mentioned earlier, which introduced a further category of "preliminary proceedings" in section 36P(1) of the Legal Profession Act, in which a foreign lawyer with full registration may appear and plead in.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Today, Singapore has established itself as a premier international dispute resolution hub in the region.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This has a direct positive repercussion on our economy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Using the words of the hon Minister, "it drives work to Singapore and for Singaporeans".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But this position is hard-won and one which we must not take for granted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is noteworthy that MinLaw had consulted extensively with various stakeholders since 2019 before introducing this Bill in Parliament in November 2021.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The effort put in by the Ministry is commendable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have three clarifications to seek from the hon Minister.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, I seek clarification on the scope of the Minister's power in clause 6 of the Bill that introduces the proposed section 115(B)(7) of the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This clause gives the Minister the power to prescribe proceedings to which lawyers may charge their fees pursuant to the CFA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For a start, it is proposed that domestic and international arbitration, certain SICC proceedings as well as its related Court proceedings and mediation proceedings be prescribed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is precisely the same grounds upon which third-party funding is available under Civil Law (Third-Party) Funding Regulations 2017.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do not have an issue with the proposed prescribed proceedings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My question relates to how the Minister intends to exercise his power in the future to extend the use of CFA in other proceedings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister, in his speech, mentioned that he is seriously considering extending CFA to domestic litigation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My question is: what would be the principal considerations?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And he mentioned access to justice is one of them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also welcome the hon Minister's point raised in his speech just now that he would be consulting stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And if he could elaborate on exactly how he proposes to consult the stakeholders, that will be most welcome.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My next question relates to how concerns expressed by the Government previously, when this issue had been mooted in the past, have been dealt with.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: When Senior Minister of State Indranee Rajah, as she then was, was asked in 2017 about the Government's position on event-triggered fee arrangements, she stated that the Government was looking into the matter but was concerned about two specific issues.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The first concern was how to deal with the potential conflict of interest that may arise on the part of the lawyer since he has a direct financial interest in the outcome of the litigation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Take, for instance, the case of a lawyer who has cashflow issues.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a result, he may decide to negotiate a settlement with a counterparty for a lower amount than what he would reasonably get for his client through a Court judgment if the matter was litigated to the end.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this case, the case would have been closed earlier, and he will get paid with an uplift under the CFA earlier too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The second concern she expressed was the prospect of increased frivolous litigation and raised litigation costs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On this point, I agree with the hon Minister Mr Edwin Tong, that the no-win-no-fee structure should already make the lawyers think twice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But I believe that there could be situations where lawyers may engage in some form of sabre-rattling to deal with acts or maybe leverage of extra legal factors, for example, the concern on the part of counterparties to stay out of courts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These factors are obviously frivolous on their own because we are talking about legal merits of the case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would be grateful if the hon Minister could please outline steps to address the concerns.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Currently, a lawyer owes a duty not to overcharge his client.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If he does so, he would be liable for misconduct and may be hauled up for disciplinary action.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is provided specifically under Rule 17 (7) of the Legal Profession (Professional Conduct) Rules 2015, which the hon Minister referred to as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under this provision, the legal practitioner must not charge any fee or disbursements, or render a bill, for an amount, which constitutes overcharging even if there is a fee agreement that permits the charging of the fee, disbursements or the amount.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I understand from the hon Minister that it is proposed the overcharging regime should also apply to a CFA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under the CFA, a lawyer may charge an uplift should there be a favourable outcome.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The question arises as to what will constitute a fair amount for the lawyers to charge as an uplift that will not be viewed as a case of overcharging.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Let us consider a case where a lawyer would have ordinarily charged $X for a case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under the CFA with his client, it is provided that, if the lawyer loses, he gets zero.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Should he win, how much can he charge as an uplift without being accused of overcharging? $2X? $3X?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would it make a difference if it is stated in the CFA that, if the lawyer loses, he may charge $0.5X instead of zero?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And it seems to me that the hon Minister, by mentioning that the risk that the lawyer assumes, can go into the issue of the reasonableness of what he can charge, that seems to be the case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We need to guard against creating perverse incentives with price signals that do not reflect the true value of services.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For many years, lawyers in Singapore are guided by the laws against maintenance and champerty.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Section 107 of the Legal Profession Act provides for an express prohibition against a lawyer having an interest in the lawsuit of his client.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Section 107 says a solicitor must not (a) purchase or agree to purchase the interest or any part of the interest of his client or of any party in any suit, action or other contentious proceeding brought or to be brought or maintained; or (b) enter into any agreement by which he is retained or employed to prosecute any suit or action or other contentious proceeding which stipulates for or contemplates payment only in the event of success in that suit, action or proceeding.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Section 107(3) provides that "A solicitor is subject to the laws of maintenance and champerty like any other person." In Rule 18 of the Legal Profession (Professional Conduct) Rules, it was stressed that "A legal practitioner or law practice must not enter into any negotiations with a client (a) for an interest in the subject matter of litigation; or (b) for remuneration proportionate to the amount which may be recovered by the client in the proceedings." Sir, the rationale of these rules is based on the conventional wisdom that the “Advocate and solicitor must maintain his independent and professional standing (unaffected by any personal interest in the outcome of a matter) in order to act effectively in representing his client’s interests.” As recent as in 2013, the Court of three Judges suspended a lawyer, Mr Kurubalan s/o Manickam Rengaraju, for six months for breaching section 107 of the Legal Profession Act and, at that time, Rule 37 of the Professional Conduct Rules because he entered into a champertous agreement with his client.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In the decision by the Court of three Judges, the Court went through the reasons for the law against champerty.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: At paragraph 40, the Court said: "Maintenance is defined as officious intermeddling in litigation (see Hill v Archbold   1 QB 686 at 693) and champerty is a particular form of maintenance where one party agrees to aid another to bring a claim on the basis that the person who gives the aid shall receive a share of what may be recovered in the action".

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I also acknowledge the explanations given by MinLaw in its media release on 1 November 2021 explaining the Government’s rationale for amending the Legal Profession Act to allow for the Conditional Fee Agreement (CFA).

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Nevertheless, I also wish to express my concern that the rationale for the rule against champerty and maintenance are still very applicable today, even if some countries have already abolished the law.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: One of the rules, as stated in Rule 4 of the Professional Conduct Rules, is the lawyer's paramount duty to the Court as an officer of the Court and this duty takes precedence over the legal practitioner’s duty to the legal practitioner’s client.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As Lord Denning observed in a 1962 judgment “in Re Trepca Mines (No 2): "The common law fears that the champertous maintainer might be tempted, for his own personal gain, to inflame the damages, to suppress evidence, or even to suborn witnesses." Sir, currently, the amendment defines "prescribed proceedings" to mean proceedings as prescribed in the regulations.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, later, if "prescribed proceedings" is extended to other forms of litigation in the future, will it result in more litigation suits because of the personal stake of the lawyers in the outcome of the lawsuits?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In 2008, 21 people were arrested in Hong Kong for champerty, maintenance and conspiracy.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: These people were recovery agents "helping" accident victims on a "no win, no fee" basis.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: One of the people arrested in Hong Kong was a lawyer.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: How would the Police deal with an unscrupulous lawyer or his agents in Singapore who may decide to stake out hospitals to look out for victims injured in road accidents or industrial accidents?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I believe there are complaints by insurance companies against lawyers or sometimes their agents who are seen as what we call “ambulance chasers”.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: These people are quick to ask the victims to sue in order to claim for more damages and legal costs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Would this group of people be able to circumvent the law by asking the accident victims to sign the CFA?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Third, who will protect the interest of the vulnerable clients if the lawyer has an interest in the outcome of the suit?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For example, if a lawyer wishes to settle the case because his legal costs are protected, then that lawyer may then insist on a settlement even though the client may disagree to the terms of settlement.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In such a case, the interest of the client and the interest of the lawyer may no longer be the same.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For uplift fees, will there be a prescribed range of uplift fees allowed?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will help level the playing field for Singapore lawyers in international dispute resolution and also increase access to justice.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are likely to be transnational, high-value commercial disputes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Ministry has indicated that it will continue to study whether CFAs can promote access to justice in other categories of proceedings, including domestic proceedings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But the consideration for cases on the other end of the spectrum – domestic cases involving indigent litigants, will be different.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In cases involving indigent litigants, there may be a greater need to be more protective of the interests of the litigant, as compared to those of parties in high-value commercial disputes who will likely be well-advised.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In establishing the overarching framework under the Bill, can the Minister share what steps the Ministry has taken to ensure that the framework is sufficiently flexible to extend to all categories of disputes?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The lessons learnt from initial applications of the CFA framework to high-value commercial disputes may have limited application to cases involving indigent litigants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How will the Ministry study the suitability of CFAs for enhancing access to justice for indigent litigants?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is about plans for allowing CFAs to act in international mediation proceedings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore has taken steps to position itself as a global mediation hub.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The passing of the Mediation Act in 2017 provided a framework for international mediation in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify whether CFAs will be allowed to act in international mediation proceedings that do not arise from permitted categories of arbitration or litigation?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point is about the classification of cases that are transmitted to other forums.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is not unusual for cases to be transmitted for hearing before different forums.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, the current Rules of Court contemplate the transfer of proceedings from the General Division of the High Court to the SICC, and vice versa.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that CFAs will only apply to certain categories of cases for a start, can the Minister clarify how the CFA framework will take into account cases that are commenced in one forum, then transmitted to another forum?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is there a possibility under the proposed CFA framework that a case may be commenced in a forum where CFAs are permitted then transmitted to another where CFAs are not permitted?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At the outset, I declare my interest as an international commercial disputes lawyer.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore is a leading international dispute resolution hub because our legal profession, judiciary and laws are not only leading the cutting edge on the forefront of legal development, but they have also adapted to keep us ahead of the curve to meet the ever-changing needs of global legal demands.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I welcome this Bill which seeks to continue to firmly strengthen Singapore’s position as an international legal and dispute resolution hub.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I will be focusing my speech on CFAs.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Since 2017, the law has already provided availability of Third Party Funding as an option in limited circumstances, for example, in international and, subsequently, domestic arbitrations.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There is already a growing trend of alternative funding methods for litigation and arbitration globally.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is especially important given the economic downturn and conservative outlook faced by many corporate clients all over the world.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On contingency fees, Prof Patricia Danzon, an American economist stated: "The common allegation that the contingent fees induces attorneys to bring claims with little legal merit has no basis in logic.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The fact that the fee depends on winning provides an incentive to screen out issues with little legal merit.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: An incentive that is lacking with an hourly fee." Further, various studies have shown that CFAs or similar arrangements discourage lawyers to take on unmeritorious cases.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The CFAs provide a financial disincentive not to commence frivolous suits or claims.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, I do have five clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, should there perhaps be a mandated cap on the uplift in certain circumstances?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is to prevent the uplift from being too disproportionate to what would have been reasonable standard of costs?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I appreciate and welcome the fact that lawyers may still be held liable for overcharging under the CFAs, pursuant to amendments under the Legal Professional Conduct Rules.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, as alluded to by Members Mr Murali Pillai and Mr Lim Biow Chuan, guidance as to how much of an uplift can also provide helpful guidance as to what is excessive or overcharging in a CFA.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the UK, contingency fees, or damages-based agreements (DBAs), have been permitted for contentious work in litigation or arbitration proceedings in England and Wales.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This means that lawyers can conduct litigation and arbitration in this jurisdiction in return for a share of any damages.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Depending on the type of cases, there are differences in the limit of cap for such a contingency fee.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If the CFAs are extended to other categories of disputes, then this cap can be adjusted downwards to reflect the greater consumer or client protection required or vulnerability of certain groups of clients in the future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A cap may also help offer the best balance to prevent legal costs from spiraling upwards and, at the same time, attract the optimal amount of disputes to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My second clarification is in relation to the resolution of disputes in CFAs.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The new section 115C states that the uplift fees will not be recoverable from the losing party in respect of party-and-party costs.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Thus, the uplift fees will have to be paid from the pocket of the client to the lawyer.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I welcome this amendment as it means that there is a lesser risk that CFAs may impact party-and-party costs and costs of litigation all around.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Bill also allows that such uplift in CFAs can also be based on reduced hourly rates, instead of a lump sum uplift.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the UK, the permissibility of such "hybrid" arrangements was not clear within its legislation and was the subject of an English Court of Appeal case which only recently clarified the position.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Given the possibility of disputes arising out of the CFAs, can I confirm if lawyers and clients can still refer their solicitor-and-client fees in the CFAs for taxation in the case of a dispute?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will be more straightforward and cost-effective than filing a separate claim in Court or arbitration for a dispute under the CFA.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My third clarification is in relation to protection of lawyers entering into CFAs.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My fourth clarification is on the duty of disclosure.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To what extent should such CFAs be disclosed by way of statutory or regulatory obligations, for example, through SGX announcements or audited yearly financial statements?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is because in an ongoing litigation or arbitration proceeding, such disclosures may cause a certain perception of pressure to succeed on the part of both the client and the party to that CFA.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This may impact the dynamics between the two competing parties or conflicting parties in the dispute, for instance.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My last clarification is centered on the protection for the client.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I understand from MinLaw's press release that safeguards will be implemented in the subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What are these safeguards to protect a client entering into CFAs and how long, perhaps, would be the cooling-off period for a client in the CFAs?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some view such arrangements as the salvation for the impecunious.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Notwithstanding my clarifications and comments, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And as a litigation lawyer, I have, from time to time, come across a situation in which a client with a genuine and reasonable commercial claim shies away from pursuing their claim due to the potential legal costs they could face if they were not successful in their action.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, all cases, regardless of the merit of the claim, have the potential of not succeeding due to various factors like the performance of witnesses or the introduction of new evidence or counterclaims.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, there is always a risk that a litigant could ultimately lose and be saddled with the costs of both its own lawyers and that of the other parties.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: A typical CFA in the UK, for example, stipulates that a lawyer acts on the basis that he will be paid nothing in fees if his client loses his case.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In the event that the client succeeds, he would be paid his normal fees, and may also earn an uplift agreed in advance, over and above the normal fees.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I support the amendment of the Act to allow for CFAs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Aside from these, there are ancillary dimensions that the relevant authorities and lawyers should consider once CFAs are allowed.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: First, the ethical considerations in structuring and offering CFAs; second, After-the-Event Insurance; and third, ensuring that lawyers retain reasonable latitude to determine the terms of their CFAs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As regards ethical considerations, lawyers are bound by duties owed to their client.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These duties may sometimes create tension with the financial pressures of running the business of a law firm.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: CFAs may exacerbate these tensions as they give the lawyer a more pronounced financial interest in the outcome of the matter underlying the CFA.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: For example, depending on the terms of the CFA, a lawyer may find himself in a situation where although it may be in the client’s interests to accept a settlement offer, it may not be in his, because he may not get paid anything.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The converse could also be true if a particular CFA treats a settlement essentially as a win – it may lead to the lawyer advising the client to take the settlement and to forego proceedings because there is a guaranteed fee to be earned as compared to going to trial or the arbitration hearing, which would still bear some risk.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This could lead to undersettling, which is an issue that has been identified in the UK’s implementation of CFAs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Ultimately, these approaches may lead to outcomes that are not the most advantageous to clients.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Practice guidelines could be introduced to guide lawyers, for example, to reduce to writing their advice to clients as regards any settlement under a CFA, so that it is unambiguous as to what exactly was the advice provided by the lawyer in the event of a possible future lawyer-client dispute.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Another area of concern would be how the concept of CFAs are communicated by law firms to clients, including on their websites and advertisements.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The use of the term "no win, no fee" may technically be correct as regards fees, but it obfuscates the fact that there would still be some cost incurred by the client, for example, filing fees and other disbursements.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: For arbitration, there would also be the costs of the tribunal.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, lawyers must be careful not to inadvertently mislead members of the public or clients that there is absolutely nothing to be paid if the litigant is not successful.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Guidelines could be drawn up by the Ministry in this regard.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Clients are also unlikely to fully understand how a CFA works, especially the terms and conditions of what constitutes a "success" and when an uplift would apply.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It is, therefore, essential that the Ministry sets out clearly the information that a lawyer would need to furnish its client when it is considering to engage a lawyer under the terms of a CFA.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Ministry could, therefore, consider drawing up pro forma documents or templates in a form that would be easily understood by members of the public, that could be mandated for use by lawyers when they discuss CFAs with clients.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The hon Minister mentioned earlier that MinLaw will be drawing up guidance together with the Law Society and I hope that my suggestions above can be taken into consideration when drafting this guide.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Another area is the risk assessment that lawyers will themselves have to do when considering whether to offer a CFA to clients and on what terms.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I would also like to suggest that some training be provided, including in the Continuous Professional Development programme, for lawyers to pick up the knowledge required to undertake this type of risk assessment and how this risk will be translated into the terms of the CFA they offer including the quantum of uplift.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: CFAs have been allowed in the United Kingdom since 1998, and I am moving on now to my next point on After-the-Event insurance.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: One feature that has emerged is the dependence of the CFA market on the existence of After-the-Event insurance or AEIs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: AEIs also allow a litigant who may have a perfectly viable case but limited financial means to obtain access to justice.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Several insurers in Singapore already offer AEIs, not only for arbitration but for civil and commercial litigation as well.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I am, however, unable to find statistics on how prevalent the use of AEIs are.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Nonetheless, AEIs are a useful feature for litigants to consider, as CFAs only ameliorate the risk of bearing their own lawyer’s fees if they lose their case, but not the opposing party’s costs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This will further the objective of access to justice, and the Ministry and the Law Society may wish to consider increasing public knowledge and understanding of this insurance.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, the use of AEIs may increase with the introduction of CFAs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I would urge the Ministry to regulate the market with a light touch to allow lawyers to negotiate terms appropriate to the complexion of each case, for example, providing for the payment of basic or interim fees, or fees arising from ancillary proceedings that were not originally envisioned when the CFA was entered into.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Provisions to make these regulations are also included in the amendments and will be rolled out by the Ministry accordingly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Before I go into addressing the specific queries raised by Members, let me just make three broad points.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The first is, we appreciate that in introducing the CFA Framework, we have moved away from some of the traditional structures that lawyers are used to – maintenance, champerty – Mr Lim spoke about it; Mr Murali Pillai as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Which is why we have chosen to do this incrementally, cautiously.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We set up a framework to deal with prescribed proceedings first, dealing with the scenario where in most, if not all, of those circumstances, the clients involved are likely to be sophisticated clients, understanding the commercial context and appreciating the need for this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And at the same time, putting our lawyers who compete with foreign lawyers for international work, on the same platform, so that they can also, like their foreign counterparts, go in to make a bid for work on the basis of using CFAs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we start with that principle and to take up Mr Murali Pillai's point, as we study, and we have not completed our study – to extend this to other proceedings, we will carefully decide, we will consult widely – and in the same way as Mr Pillai has said we have done leading up to this Bill, we will continue to do so – all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will decide at that stage whether an extension is appropriate and if so, with what kind of additional criteria as safeguards.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As Members would know, even with this framework that we have put in a cautious manner for sophisticated clients, we are already putting in safeguards here.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, that is the first point that I would make about the framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The second point is that I have heard several comments about the agreement: should we regulate the agreement, should we put this in pro forma or should we put in some standard terms?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I also heard Mr Raj Joshua Thomas said earlier that we should also have a fee structure that allows lawyers to negotiate and that, in his words, is best "appropriate to the complexion of the case".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This, really, is the raison d'etre behind the CFA – to let the parties decide what are the triggering requirements to allow a party to decide when an uplift would be appropriate, depending on the context of the particular case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And it is in this context that the interest of the lawyer and the client can best be aligned – not separated, but best be aligned.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Despite that, we continue to have oversight over the agreement because, just as we have done in Part 8 of the LPA for agreed fees, not CFAs but agreed fees, the Court continues to retain a discretion to have an inquiry into, and oversight of, these agreements.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Likewise, in the context of the CFA, that remains the same.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the Courts will still have oversight of the uplift, and in Mr Murali Pillai's words: "to determinate based on the reasonableness of the case, the context of the circumstances, the relevant weightage of the risks taken, the complexity of the case, the length of the case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All of these are factors which the Court takes into account.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Which is why it would not be possible upfront to state, you can only uplift by X, or 2X, or 3X", because it may be appropriate in some cases, it may not be appropriate in other cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, that is the second point I will make.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The third point I will make is that throughout Members' speeches, I have heard that because this is a new development in our framework, we should be giving guidance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Certainly, we have committed to doing so upfront.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is the reason why we have consulted extensively, both open as well as closed, and we will continue to do so and work with Law Society to ensure that lawyers and users alike, clients, are familiar with the framework and, as far as we can, provide guidance which does not tie the hands of solicitors as they negotiate these CFAs but, at the same time, give guidance as to what the framework requires of the CFAs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The potential benefits that CFAs can offer in the use of mediation have to be viewed against the interplay between international mediation proceedings and domestic mediation and litigation proceedings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, for instance, at present, there is no clear delineation in existing legislation between mediation proceedings that are "international" and those that are "domestic".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If parties to an "international" mediation do not reach a settlement, the dispute may proceed to be heard in the SICC or the High Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As CFAs will presently not be permitted in the High Court, this may then create an ambiguity for lawyers and litigants, given that proceedings on one stream in the High Court will not be allowed for CFAs and those at the SICC will be allowed for CFAs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Further, mediation proceedings that are more domestic in nature may involve litigants of a wide range of profiles that need differentiated treatment and protection, for the reasons I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And so, this requires some further study and consideration.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, Mr Louis Ng asked how the CFA framework will take into account cases that are commenced in one forum and transferred to another, and whether it is possible that a case may be commenced in a forum where CFAs are permitted and then transferred to another forum where CFAs are not permitted.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Where proceedings are transferred between two fora in which CFAs are allowed – for instance, from arbitration to related Court or mediation proceedings – then, obviously, the CFAs will continue in the case of the solicitor and the client.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, CFAs will be allowed in those circumstances.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will study this further and consider whether we should change this, but as a starting point, under this framework, as long as one of the proceedings, either from which it is transferred or to which it is transferred, does not allow the CFA, then the CFA will not be allowed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This approach towards CFAs and the transfer of forums will avoid any unintended consequences and risks to litigants arising from CFAs, and we will make clear the position in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about the circumstances of enforcement by the Court, with reference to the proposed section 115D(4) and (7) of the Bill he mentioned.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The sections referenced by Mr Murali Pillai are aligned with the current 113(3) and 113(7) of the current LPA, in terms of the Court’s powers to deal with contentious cost agreements.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I made the point earlier that parties should have freedom of contract to negotiate the terms of the CFA – and it should be enforced by the Court like any contract if the requirements in the proposed 115B of this Bill, which sets out the regulatory framework and the requirements of the CFAs in this case, have been complied with; and also, of course, if the CFA is not found to be void or voidable for one of the grounds listed in 115D.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On taxation of solicitor-and-client costs under the CFA, Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim asked whether the taxation process in Court will still be applicable in respect of solicitor-and-client costs under a CFA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: He also asked if disputes regarding the validity of CFAs would fall under the scrutiny of taxation proceedings, or if they should be subject to separate Court or arbitration proceedings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is provided under section 115C(5) of the Bill and it is similar to the position for contentious business agreements under the current section 112(4) of the LPA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If there are questions, however, on the validity or the effect of a CFA, parties should bring an application to Court under section 115D(2) of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Under section 115D(5) of the Bill, if the Court finds that the CFA either does not satisfy the statutory requirements or is found to be void or voidable, then the costs under the CFA can then be assessed in accordance with the rules applicable to taxation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim also sought confirmation that lawyers agreeing to CFAs would not be held personally liable for adverse party-and-party costs under a CFA, unless there are circumstances of personal or professional conduct that attracts personal liability for costs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will also be clarified in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim’s query about the disclosure of CFAs vis-à-vis regulatory obligations, such as SGX announcements or audited financial statements, let me reiterate again a point I made at the start of the reply speech, that CFAs really are an additional fee structure.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is an agreement that allows lawyers and their clients to work out a fee structure.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: CFAs are not intended to change, nor do they change, any existing statutory or regulatory obligations relating to disclosure, from what is expected if normal fee agreements are entered into by companies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, in assessing whether you need to make an announcement, the usual criteria will apply, whether it is material in the particular context of the circumstances of that particular announcement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Companies and lawyers will still have to make an assessment and assess the extent to which a CFA will need to be disclosed, in the context of existing guidelines and the regulations governing disclosures.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked how concerns relating to CFAs that had been highlighted in the past – I think Mr Murali Pillai cited some past speeches and examples – had been addressed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, dealing with potential conflicts of interest, I had again mentioned how, in the context of a proper CFA, in this case at least, the sense is that the interest between a solicitor and his client in the CFA can be aligned.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But to Mr Murali Pillai's point about a potential conflict arising because of a direct financial interest in the outcome of the litigation, Mr Murali Pillai also asked whether the lawyer may advise on a settlement instead of litigation in order to settle the matter earlier and receive payment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is notwithstanding that the client will receive a lower amount than what he may reasonably expect if the matter proceeds to litigation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas also highlighted a similar scenario.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If parties have an agreement and you choose to decide that there will be a payment based on a settlement, then, obviously, if you define the terms of the settlement not below a certain amount, or at least containing these terms, that will protect the client's interest, to ensure that there is no under-settling in this case; not just any settlement, but a settlement that comports with the client's interest in the outcome.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Under a CFA, the standard expected of a lawyer in advising how a case should be conducted or proceeded on remains the same as that of a normal fee agreement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, what I said earlier in my opening speech about the relevance of the legal professional (PCR) rules, they continue to apply.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Among others, Rule 17 of the PCR requires lawyers to explain a proposal of settlement clearly and properly to the client; or any other offer or position taken by another party, which affects the client.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the same time, the lawyer must also evaluate, together with the client, whether any consequence of a matter justifies the expense or the risk to be undertaken.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, if you choose to proceed with the case, there must be an assessment by the lawyer that this would be in the best interest of the client, bearing in mind, obviously, that, in litigation, there are various vicissitudes that you cannot control – points which Mr Raj Joshua Thomas and several other Members highlighted.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If there is a reasonable prospect of the client recovering a higher sum of money in litigation, as compared to settling the matter, such that pursuing litigation would justify the expense of doing so, the lawyer would be obliged to advise his client of the same.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These are principles which many of the lawyers who have spoken would be familiar with.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In CFAs, the remuneration of lawyers depends on the successful outcome of the cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Generally, lawyers are also rational economic actors and they would likely have little commercial reason to support frivolous or weak litigation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The risk of little or no likelihood of monetary return for their efforts would not be commercially justifiable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Further, as the lawyers may have to fund the litigation until its conclusion, or at least a portion of it, there is likely to be less tendency to pursue all possible avenues at any cost and a greater tendency to be more cost-conscious on the contrary and cost-effective.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the same time, to assuage Members, the experiences of other jurisdictions also lend support to this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members might recall that I said earlier that we took a cautious approach.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We studied the approach in other jurisdictions and learned from their experiences.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A study on the impact of CFAs in clinical negligence cases over a period of 10 years showed that there has been an increase in cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But, over a period of 10 years from 2006 to 2017, even in Singapore, we saw an increase in cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it is not because of the CFAs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But what is important is that the proportion of successful claims in this period did not change.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In fact, there were more successful claims funded by CFAs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This underscores the role of the CFAs in enabling the pursuit of meritorious claims.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Studies in Australia have also showed that there had not been a significant uptick in unmeritorious suits since the introduction in their jurisdiction of the CFAs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And we believe that Singapore’s experience is not likely to be different.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On whether litigation costs will be raised, let me reiterate that existing professional obligations continue to apply, and this includes the rules against overcharging.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Even if the CFA provides for the payment of an agreed fees, the PCR prohibits overcharging – a point I made earlier – even in a context of today's rules on agreed fee without the uplift.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If the lawyer cannot in good faith charge the fee, taking into account factors, such as the nature of the work done or legal work concerned and the time necessary to undertake the legal work – points which Mr Murali Pillai made – then, these are factors which will be taken into account by the Court when assessing the veracity of the agreed fee.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We believe that legal costs will continue to be moderated and also adjusted by the market itself.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If a client finds that a lawyer’s fees are too high, they are free to engage another lawyer who may offer a different range of fees and different uplift formula.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Lawyers are also free to adjust their fee arrangements to better place themselves in competition.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And Mr Raj Joshua Thomas had himself alluded to this, in urging for lawyers to be allowed to negotiate terms appropriate to the complexion of the particular case concerned.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked what would constitute a fair amount for lawyers to charge as an uplift, so that this will not be viewed as a case of overcharging.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But save for that, I think as Mr Pillai says, look at the reasonableness in the context of each case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would say that the mere fact that there is an uplift is not a reason for setting aside the agreement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is the whole raison d'etre behind the CFA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would add a further point that when you have limits on uplift fees in other jurisdictions, they are typically legislated because the fee arrangement in those jurisdictions extend to access to justice type of litigants.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They help access to justice indigent litigants to access the courts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And in those cases, you will more likely find a cap on the amount to which you can uplift.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In this case, at least at the start of our framework, we do not apply the framework to those types of cases and those types of litigants.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And so, in our case here, we do not need to put a limit on the fee arrangements and the uplift amounts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But as I mentioned earlier, if we extend our framework into other types of cases, this will be a fresh consideration that we will review at the appropriate time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Zhulkarnain asked about other protection mechanisms for litigants and what safeguards are available for a litigant who had entered into a CFA with a lawyer and thereafter changes lawyers; or whose lawyer decides to withdraw from the case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: My first response really is to ensure that, as you prepare the CFA, structure the terms which will cater for these eventualities.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Sometimes, parties change lawyers; sometimes, there might be changes in the way in which the case proceeds.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is best to ensure that, as far as possible, in terms of an agreement, you cater for these scenarios upfront.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, lawyers and their clients should discuss and provide for how and when the CFA may be terminated, and if it is terminated before the conclusion of the case, how would the remuneration structure and what triggering conditions will apply in those cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And this, I would say, is no different from current traditional fee agreement that is based on either time cost or conclusion of some milestones and so on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, parties should deal with this as a matter of agreement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Either party can apply to the Court and the Court will have the same power to enforce or set aside the agreement as if the change had not occurred, having regard to the relevant terms of the CFA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: With regard to fees payable to the first lawyer, the Court may order the amount due in respect of anything done by the lawyer under the CFA to be assessed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, there could be a scenario where, before the conclusion of the case, a lawyer is discharged but a substantial amount of work is done.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
